transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thanks for seeing me. I came in because... I don't know, for a long time now there's just been this heavy, low feeling sitting on me most days. I'm still getting through my driving routes, though. I drive a truck, mostly regional, and let me tell you, the traffic on the interstate lately has been an absolute joke. They've had this one lane closed for construction for what feels like three years, and it just backs everything up for miles. I sit there burning daylight just staring at the bumper in front of me. 

Anyway, I still do that, and I still make it to my volunteer shifts at the animal shelter. We actually just got a litter of beagle mixes in that chew on absolutely everything. One of them got ahold of my good work boots last Tuesday and just went to town on the laces. But yeah, even with all that going on, it just feels like I'm going through the motions. Like I'm not really present in my own life, you know? Just... heavy.
Do you still find joy in the things you used to enjoy, like volunteering at the animal shelter?

I mean, I don't know if "joy" is the right word anymore. I still go, but... it's just something I do. Like, I'll be there cleaning out the kennels or walking them, and it's fine, but I don't get that spark from it like I used to. Speaking of the kennels, they just switched the brand of cleaner they use, and man, it smells like straight industrial bleach mixed with cheap pine needles. It gives me a headache if I'm in the back room for too long. I told the manager, Sarah—she's a nice lady, used to work at the post office before she retired—I told her we need to go back to the old stuff. She said it's a budget thing, which I get, you know? Everything's getting more expensive. Even diesel for my truck is up another ten cents this week. But yeah, the shelter... I just kind of show up and do the work, and then I go home.
Do you ever feel pleasure or happiness at all anymore?

I mean... I don't really know. It's hard to say what happiness even feels like these days. I guess maybe not really? Like, I stopped at this diner off Route 81 the other day, right? Place is supposed to have the best meatloaf. I used to really look forward to a good meatloaf, you know, with the ketchup glaze baked on top like my mom used to make. But this place, they put some kind of weird brown gravy all over it. Swear it looked just like 10W-30 motor oil. And the waitress, she was nice enough, but she kept calling me "hon" in this real high-pitched voice. Sounded exactly like my ex-wife's sister, Brenda. Man, Brenda had this little toy poodle that just barked at the wind. I swear that dog didn't sleep, ever. We had to watch it for a week back in '08 and it chewed up all the wooden baseboards in our front hallway. Cost me a couple hundred bucks from my security deposit when we finally moved out of that rental... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, feeling happy. Yeah, I don't know. I just don't really feel much of anything most of the time. Just flat, I guess.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, low feeling?

Well, let's see... it's been a long time. I'd say about three years now. Yeah, right around the time my dad passed away. That was a tough time. We had his service out at this little cemetery near the county line, and I remember it was raining so hard the mud was up to our ankles. Ruined a perfectly good pair of dress shoes I bought just for the occasion. They were those slip-ons, you know, with the little tassels? I thought they looked sharp, but they just soaked right through. 

I tried to clean them up afterwards with this leather polish I got from a guy at the truck stop, but they never looked the same. That guy at the truck stop, though, he was a real character. Sold everything out of the back of his rig—CB radios, bootleg DVDs, you name it. He tried to sell me this oversized steering wheel cover that looked like leopard print. I told him, "Buddy, I'm driving a Peterbilt, not a disco ball." But anyway, yeah, it's been about three years since my dad died, and that heavy feeling just kind of set in and never really left.
Are there any activities that you still enjoy or look forward to?

I mean... not really. I don't really look forward to much of anything these days. It's just kind of wake up, get through the day, go to sleep. Same old routine. You know, speaking of routines, they just changed up my route at work. Used to be I'd take the 95 straight down, hit the same three stops by noon. Now they've got me cutting through these back roads, and let me tell you, the potholes on County Road 9 are something else. I hit one last Tuesday that practically rattled my teeth loose. Spilled half my coffee right onto the dashboard. And it wasn't even the good coffee, it was that cheap stuff from the breakroom that tastes like burnt popcorn. 

I tried telling dispatch about the roads, this guy named Gary. Gary's always eating those little powdered donuts, you know the ones? Gets the white dust all over his keyboard. I told him, "Gary, you're gonna break an axle sending guys down that road." He just sort of shrugged and took another bite. Honestly, I don't think he even listens half the time. But yeah, as far as looking forward to things... I just don't. It's all just kind of flat.
Have you experienced any periods of even a few days where you felt significantly better than you do now?

I don't think so. No, not really. It's just been this same low feeling, day in, day out. Never really lifts, you know? Not even for a weekend. Weekends used to be when I'd get the truck washed. There was this place off exit 42, hand-wash only. The guy who ran it, Sal, he had this old pressure washer that sounded like a jet engine taking off. You could hear it from the highway. Sal was always trying to sell me on these "premium wax" packages. Said it would make the rig shine like a new penny. I finally bought it once, back in... maybe 2018? Cost me forty bucks extra. And wouldn't you know it, it rained the very next morning. Just my luck, right? Rained so hard the wipers couldn't keep up. That's the thing about weather around here, it just turns on a dime. Like last week, they said it was going to be sunny, and I ended up driving through a hail storm near Scranton. Sounded like gravel hitting the roof. 

But, uh... no. No periods where I felt better. It's just been the same heavy feeling the whole time.
Are there any things that you still find pleasure in, even if it's just a little bit?

Not really... no. I can't really think of anything that brings me any kind of joy right now. I used to like grabbing a hot meal at the end of a long haul, but lately food is just food, you know? There used to be this diner I'd always hit up right off I-80. Marge's Diner. She made this meatloaf that was just out of this world. Smothered in onions and brown gravy. 

But she sold the place a couple years back to this guy from Chicago, and he came in and completely changed the menu. Started putting avocado on everything. I mean, who puts avocado on a turkey club? It just slides right out the sides when you take a bite. Makes a huge mess on the steering wheel if you are trying to eat while you drive. I had to use half a roll of paper towels to get the grease off my hands last time I stopped there. And those paper towels they sell at the Pilot stations now, they are completely useless. One wipe and they just disintegrate. It is like trying to clean up with cheap tissue paper. You end up with little white fuzzies all over your hands and the gearshift. 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, enjoying things. Yeah, no. Nothing really gives me that spark anymore. It is all just kind of gray.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Yeah, I guess so. I mean, like I said, I don't really care about much anymore. Even the stuff I used to like... it's just a chore now. Take fishing, right? I used to love taking the boat out on Lake Hopatcong. Get out there before the sun comes up, just you and the water. It was quiet. 

But then they started building all those new condos on the east shore. Just massive, ugly things blocking the view. And the traffic on Route 15 getting up there on a Saturday? Forget about it. It's bumper to bumper all the way from Jefferson. Last time I went, I sat behind this guy hauling a camper who kept riding his brakes the whole way up the mountain. I could smell burning brake pads for three miles. And you know how much a brake job costs on a rig these days? My mechanic, Dave, he quoted me twelve hundred just for the front axle. Twelve hundred! And Dave's supposed to be giving me the buddy discount because we went to high school together. We were in shop class with Mr. Henderson. Henderson was missing half his index finger from a bandsaw accident... 

Anyway, I haven't taken the boat out in... I don't even know. Months. I just don't have the energy or the interest to deal with it all anymore. It's easier to just stay home.
Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite or sleep patterns?

My appetite is about the same, I guess. But sleep... sleep's a different story. On nights before a run, I'll just lie there in the dark, thinking about all the stops I have to make the next day. Or I'll wake up around four in the morning and that's it, I can't really get back to sleep. My alarm clock has those big red numbers, the kind that are way too bright. I bought it at this hardware store in town, Miller's Hardware. Old man Miller used to run it, but his son took over a few years ago. The son, he doesn't know a Phillips head from a flathead, I swear. I went in there looking for a specific kind of sealant for the truck's weather stripping, and he tried to sell me bathroom caulk. Bathroom caulk! Can you imagine that holding up on the interstate at 70 miles an hour? The wind would just rip it right off. And speaking of wind, the crosswinds on the George Washington Bridge have been brutal lately. If you're running empty, you feel every single gust. You have to grip the wheel so tight your knuckles turn white. 

But anyway, yeah, because of the sleep thing, even when I make it to work on time, I feel like I'm starting the day already worn down. Just exhausted before I even turn the key.
Are there any small things that happen during your day that you look forward to?

Look forward to? No, not really. I mean, I can't think of a single thing. It's just the exact same routine every single day. 

I used to kinda look forward to my morning coffee, getting it from this little drive-thru shack on Route 9. The lady working there always knew I wanted it black with two sugars. But they tore it down a few months ago to build another one of those massive chain pharmacies. Like we really need another pharmacy. There's already one on every single corner. And the parking lots for those places are always designed terribly if you're driving anything bigger than a sedan. They put those concrete parking blocks right where you need to swing wide. I caught my rear tire on one last month and it took a chunk right out of the sidewall. 

Do you know how hard it is to get a decent tire replaced when you're out on the road? You call dispatch and they put you on hold for twenty minutes, listening to that awful elevator music that sounds like it's being played underwater. My dispatcher, Gary, he's completely useless anyway. He's always too busy managing his fantasy football team to actually do his job. Last week he routed me right through downtown Scranton during some kind of street fair. I'm sitting there in a 53-foot trailer trying not to run over a funnel cake stand. 

But, uh, yeah. No. To answer your question, there's nothing I really look forward to. The days just kind of blur together into one long drive.
Do you feel like you no longer enjoy things that you used to find pleasurable most of the time?

I mean... didn't you just ask me that? About losing interest in stuff? I thought I just said that about the fishing. Like I said, it's all just a chore now. I don't really enjoy much of anything most days. It's just... flat. 

Like, even when I'm off the road and I could be doing something, I just sit there. The television's on, but I'm not really watching it. They have these shows on now, these reality shows about people doing the exact same job I do. Ice Road Truckers, stuff like that. Who watches that? I do it for a living, why would I want to watch someone else do it on TV? And half the time, the stuff they show isn't even realistic. They make a big deal out of sliding on a little patch of ice. Try hitting black ice on I-80 in Pennsylvania with a full load of steel coils behind you. That'll wake you up faster than a pot of truck stop coffee. I knew a guy, Tommy... he hauled steel out of Pittsburgh. He hit a patch of ice near Clarion and those coils shifted. Snapped the chains right off. They had to bring out two heavy wreckers just to clear the highway. They shut down the eastbound lanes for eight hours. Eight hours! Can you imagine being stuck in that backup? You can't even get out to stretch your legs because it's freezing, and you're just burning diesel to stay warm... 

But yeah, like I said before. I don't really enjoy things anymore. It's just easier not to bother.
Do you feel your low mood is interfering with your ability to work or perform daily activities?

Well, I mean, I'm still showing up for work, if that's what you mean. I still get the routes done. I still go down to the food pantry on the weekends like I usually do, but... man, everything just takes so much more pushing than it used to. It's like dragging a heavy tarp over a load of lumber in the rain. 

Speaking of lumber, the yard I pick up from over in Jersey, they changed their whole loading procedure last month. Used to be you'd just pull up to the bay, hand your slip to the forklift guy—this guy named Sal, great guy, always had a joke—and he'd load you up in ten minutes flat. Now they've got this new automated system where you have to scan a barcode on your phone before you even get past the gate. Half the time the scanner doesn't work if there's a glare from the sun, and you're just sitting there blocking traffic while some kid in a neon vest tries to manually type in a twenty-digit number. And don't get me started on the forklift guys they have now. Sal retired, moved down to Florida. Bought a little place in Sarasota, I think. Or maybe it was Naples. Somewhere on the Gulf Coast. Anyway, the new guys, they drop the pallets so hard you can feel the whole cab shake. I had to get out and yell at one of them last week because he almost took my mirror off. Mirrors on these rigs aren't cheap, you know. You crack one of those convex mirrors and dispatch acts like you just asked them to pay for a new engine. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, work. Yeah, I'm still doing it. But I actually started filling out an application for a logistics supervisor position a while back. Get me off the road, you know? Put me behind a desk. But I just left it sitting there unfinished. I look at it and I just... I don't trust myself to keep up with it right now. It just feels like too much.
Do you feel that your low mood is more than half the day, most days?

Well, yeah, that's kind of why I came in. I mean, I'm still getting through my routes and doing my volunteer shifts at the food pantry, but... there's just this heavy, low feeling sitting on me. Most days. More than half the day, definitely. It's like I'm just going through the motions instead of really being in my own life. 

It reminds me of this one rig I drove back in the nineties. An old Freightliner. The suspension on that thing was completely shot. Every time you hit a bump on the Cross Bronx Expressway, you'd feel it right in your teeth. And the seat—the air ride in the seat was busted, so it just sat all the way at the bottom. You'd be driving for ten hours feeling like you were dragging the undercarriage on the asphalt. I told the shop mechanic about it—this guy named Earl, missing half his left index finger from a fan belt incident—and he just told me to put a phone book under me. A phone book! Like that's going to fix a busted air seat. Try finding a phone book these days anyway. Everything's on the internet. My niece showed me how to look up restaurants on my phone, but half the time the screen is so small I end up tapping the wrong thing. I ordered a pizza once and accidentally got it with anchovies because my thumb hit the wrong little box on the screen. Who even eats anchovies? They smell like bait. 

But yeah, that heavy feeling... it's just there. Most of the time. Just weighing me down while I try to get through the day.
How many days a week do you feel this heavy, low feeling?

I mean, most days. Probably five, maybe six days out of the week. That's really why I came in, honestly. Because for a long time now, I’ve just been getting through my routes and my volunteer shifts, but there’s this heavy, low feeling sitting on me most of the time. Like I’m just going through the motions instead of really being in my own life. 

Actually, at the food pantry last Saturday, we got this huge donation from one of the big chain supermarkets. But you wouldn't believe the stuff they send over. It's all the dented cans and weird stuff nobody buys. We got three cases of canned water chestnuts and like fifty jars of pickled beets. Who eats pickled beets anyway? My grandmother used to can them herself. She had this dark, damp cellar in her old house in Scranton, and she'd keep hundreds of mason jars down there. That cellar always smelled like wet dirt and vinegar. I hated going down there to fetch things for her. They had this ancient oil furnace that would kick on and sound like a freight train crashing through the wall. Scared the absolute daylights out of me when I was a kid. I used to run back up those rickety wooden stairs so fast I'd trip and skin my knees on the edge of the steps... 

But, uh, yeah. To answer your question... most days. Almost every day of the week, really, I just have that heavy feeling.
Can you think of any activity, no matter how small, that you still find pleasure in?

Well, I... I don't know. I can't really think of anything off the top of my head. Even the stuff I used to like just feels like work now. Like, I used to really enjoy washing my truck on a Sunday morning. Getting the chrome all polished up. I had this special chamois cloth I bought at a truck stop in Ohio—one of those massive ones with the showers and the little diner inside. Best meatloaf I ever had was at that diner. The waitress there, I think her name was Barb, she'd always slip me an extra dinner roll. They had those really soft yeast rolls, you know? The kind that just melt when you put butter on them. I haven't had a good roll like that in years. The bakery down the street from my apartment tries, but they always overbake them. They get all crusty on the bottom, and if you try to make a sandwich out of it, it just falls apart in your hands. I bought a dozen last Thanksgiving and ended up throwing half of them out to the pigeons in the park. Those pigeons will eat anything, I swear. I saw one eat a whole French fry once. Just swallowed it whole. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right, stuff I enjoy. Yeah, no, I can't really think of anything right now. Nothing really stands out.
Can you describe how this heavy, low feeling affects your daily functioning and relationships?

Well, I'm still showing up. I mean, I get to work, I do my routes, I go to the pantry... but everything just takes so much more pushing than it used to. It's like walking through wet cement. I actually started filling out an application for a logistics supervisor position a while back. It's been sitting on my kitchen table for weeks. I just... I don't trust myself to keep up with it right now. 

Speaking of that kitchen table, it's this old oak thing I bought at a flea market out in Lancaster county maybe fifteen years ago. The guy who sold it to me swore it was Amish-made, but I found a 'Made in Taiwan' sticker under one of the legs when I was moving it in. Still, it's a solid table. Heavy as all get-out. I had to get my neighbor, Stan, to help me carry it up the stairs. Stan's a good guy, but he's got this weird habit of whistling show tunes whenever he's doing physical labor. We're hauling this massive piece of wood up three flights, sweating buckets, and he's just whistling 'Hello, Dolly!' the whole way up. He's got a parrot, too, an African Grey, and I swear that bird learned to whistle the exact same tunes. You can hear it through the wall sometimes. Just randomly whistling Broadway hits at two in the morning. I tried complaining to the landlord, but the landlord is this guy who lives down in Florida and only cares if the rent check clears. He's got this property management company that never actually fixes anything. I had a leaky faucet for three months before I finally just went to the hardware store and bought the washer to fix it myself. The guy at the hardware store tried to sell me a whole new sink... 

But yeah, the heavy feeling... it just makes everything harder. I get my stuff done, but I don't have the energy for anything extra, like that supervisor application.
For how many months have you been feeling this heavy, low feeling?

Well, it's been a while now. I'd say about three years. It really started after my father passed away. We had to clean out his house, and let me tell you, that man never threw a single thing away. He had this garage out back, just packed to the rafters with old car parts, newspapers from the seventies, and coffee cans full of bent nails. I spent three weekends just sorting through the coffee cans. He drank that Chock full o'Nuts brand, you know? The one in the yellow and black can. I can still smell it when I think about it. He used to make a pot every morning at 4:30 AM before he went to work at the mill. The mill closed down back in '98, I think. Turned it into one of those fancy loft apartment buildings with exposed brick and ductwork everywhere. I delivered a package there once, and the guy who signed for it was wearing a bathrobe at two in the afternoon. Had a little dog, too, one of those fluffy white ones that looks like a cotton ball. The dog kept yapping at my boots. I wear these steel-toe Red Wings for work—had 'em resoled twice already. Good boots are hard to find these days. Everything's made so cheap now, the soles wear out in six months and you're slipping on the loading dock...

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, it's been about three years since my dad died that I've felt this way.
Do you feel like you've lost the ability to experience pleasure from activities that normally would bring you happiness?

Well, I... I don't know if I've completely lost the ability. It's just hard to say. I guess I haven't really noticed if I have or not. It's not like a switch flipped, you know? It's more like... well, speaking of switches, the dome light in my rig has been acting up lately. It flickers every time I hit a pothole, and let me tell you, Interstate 80 is basically just one long pothole this time of year. The state says they're going to repave it, but they've been saying that since my nephew was in middle school, and he just graduated from Penn State last spring. Got a degree in agricultural science, if you can believe it. Wants to start a hydroponic tomato farm. He tried growing some in his dorm room once, set up all these purple grow lights. His roommate thought he was growing something illegal and called the RA. Turned out it was just cherry tomatoes. They were actually pretty good, though. A little sweet for my taste, but good on a salad. I used to make a big salad every Sunday night to take for lunches during the week. Used to chop up cucumbers, bell peppers, maybe some hard-boiled eggs... 

But, uh, what did you ask me? About losing the ability to feel happy? Yeah, I don't know. I just haven't really thought about it like that.
Can you think of any activity that you still find pleasure in, no matter how small it may seem?

I mean... I don't really know. I haven't really been paying attention to what gives me pleasure, I guess. I just sort of get through the day. Like yesterday, I was driving my route, and I usually stop at this diner off Exit 42. The Silver Spoon, it's called. They used to have this waitress there, Brenda, who always knew my order before I even sat down. Two eggs over easy, wheat toast, and a side of corned beef hash. But Brenda retired last year, moved down to Myrtle Beach to be near her grandkids. She sent me a postcard once, had a picture of a pelican on it. Those birds are weird, you know? The way they just scoop up fish in that giant pouch. I saw a documentary about them once on PBS. I used to watch a lot of PBS on Sunday afternoons. They had this guy, Bob Ross, painting those happy little trees. He made it look so easy. I bought a paint set once, thinking I'd give it a try. Got the canvas, the brushes, all those little tubes of oil paint. It smelled like turpentine in my apartment for a week. I tried painting a mountain, but it ended up looking like a gray triangle with a smudge on top. I put it in the closet and haven't looked at it since. 

So, yeah... I don't really know what to tell you about finding pleasure in things. I just haven't really noticed.
